tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep selector -A2
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Optional: send repeated requests through the Service and check headers/content or pod logs to observe approximate 50/50 distribution.

- To shift traffic: scale replicas (e.g., scale canary to 1 and stable to 3 for ~25/75), or use a more advanced traffic-weighting mechanism (Ingress/Service mesh) if needed.

What I deployed and changed
- Canary deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)

  - Replicas: 2

  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Ready
- Service endpoints: 4 pod endpoints on port 8080 (both deployments)

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep selector -A2
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Optional: send repeated requests through the Service and check headers/content or pod logs to observe approximate 50/50 distribution.

Adjusting or rolling back
- To shift traffic: scale replicas (e.g., scale canary to 1 and stable to 3 for ~25/75), or use a more advanced traffic-weighting mechanism (Ingress/Service mesh) if needed.
- To roll back immediately: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale engine-v2-1 to 0.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment had command/args set to: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which made the container exit immediately and the pod go into BackOff.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the bad command/args.
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
- imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
- Exposed containerPort 8080 (the unprivileged nginx listens on 8080 by default).

Validation
- New pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-6bb64775d-kpr7f: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts

If you need a different startup command or to serve on another port, tell me and I’ll adjust the Deployment.

Done. Your pod is now running.

What I fixed
- Root cause: The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non‑existent StorageClass "sc" (event: “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”), leaving the claim unbound and the pod Pending.
- Fix applied:
  - Recreated the PVC using an existing StorageClass: csi-hostpath-sc.
  - Recreated homepage-pod to use the bound PVC.

Current state
- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod → Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- PVC: homepage-ns/homepage-pvc → Bound to PV pvc-fa3415ab-a268-48a7-b138-ec4ee9f2df22, StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc, size 1Gi.

If you prefer to use a different StorageClass (e.g., your cluster’s default “standard”), tell me and I can switch the claim and pod accordingly. To verify locally:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pod homepage-pod (to see events and volume mounts)

  - Recreated homepage-pod to use the bound PVC.

- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod → Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- PVC: homepage-ns/homepage-pvc → Bound to PV pvc-fa3415ab-a268-48a7-b138-ec4ee9f2df22, StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc, size 1Gi.

If you prefer to use a different StorageClass (e.g., your cluster’s default “standard”), tell me and I can switch the claim and pod accordingly. To verify locally:

Root cause
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready) and to the wrong port.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the pod and Service were configured for port 80, causing connection refused on probes and no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set a named container port http on 8080.
  - Updated liveness and readiness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to http (8080). Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-68c747dfb9-4jscv — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then open http://localhost:8080
- Or, from inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

Want me to expose it externally? I can create an Ingress/Route or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service if you let me know how you’d like it accessed.

- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready) and to the wrong port.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the pod and Service were configured for port 80, causing connection refused on probes and no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set a named container port http on 8080.
  - Updated liveness and readiness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to http (8080). Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-68c747dfb9-4jscv — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then open http://localhost:8080
- Or, from inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

Want me to expose it externally? I can create an Ingress/Route or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service if you let me know how you’d like it accessed.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
        # Fix probes to use a valid path for nginx
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 3
          successThreshold: 1
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 3
          successThreshold: 1

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready) and to the wrong port.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the pod and Service were configured for port 80, causing connection refused on probes and no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set a named container port http on 8080.
  - Updated liveness and readiness probes to GET / on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to http (8080). Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-68c747dfb9-4jscv — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.32:8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then open http://localhost:8080
- Or, from inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

Want me to expose it externally? I can create an Ingress/Route or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service if you let me know how you’d like it accessed.

- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, and watch on core/v1 pods.
- Your RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to that Role, so no change was needed there.

Current Role rules
- apiGroups: [""]
- resources: ["pods"]
- verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or use the pod-reader token to call GET /api/v1/namespaces/simple-rbac-setup/pods

Note
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need pod list across all namespaces, we’ll switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments in the apps API group, not pods. Pods are in the core API group ("").

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, and watch on core/v1 pods.
- Your RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to that Role, so no change was needed there.

Current Role rules
- apiGroups: [""]
- resources: ["pods"]
- verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or use the pod-reader token to call GET /api/v1/namespaces/simple-rbac-setup/pods

Note
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need pod list across all namespaces, we’ll switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments in the apps API group, not pods. Pods are in the core API group ("").

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, and watch on core/v1 pods.
- Your RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to that Role, so no change was needed there.

Current Role rules
- apiGroups: [""]
- resources: ["pods"]
- verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or use the pod-reader token to call GET /api/v1/namespaces/simple-rbac-setup/pods

Note
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need pod list across all namespaces, we’ll switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: Service nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment labels pods with app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints and EndpointSlice were empty), so it couldn’t route traffic.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, while the Service targetPort was 80. Even with correct endpoints, traffic to container port 80 would fail.

What I changed
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (container’s listen port)
  - kept Service port at 80/TCP so clients can use http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80

Verification
- Endpoints now present: 10.244.0.33:8080 for Service web/nginx.
- From a test pod in the web namespace, curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ returns HTTP 200.

Notes
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can expose it via:
  - NodePort Service,
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it), or
  - Ingress (recommended, with an Ingress controller).
  
Tell me which exposure method you prefer and I’ll set it up.

Summary of findings
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster has no node with that label. The scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
- Why connection to the Service was refused: The web-app pods listen on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged default), but the Service was targeting port 80. That mismatch caused connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-6nq5x (Running)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-d4bhl (Running)

2) Fixed Service port mismatch
- Verified the pods serve HTTP on 8080.
- Updated Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service to targetPort: 8080 (Service port remains 80).
- Result: Service now returns the NGINX welcome page. A test curl from an in-cluster pod to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 succeeds.

Verification performed
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods shows both replicas Running.
- Endpoints for web-app-service point to both pods.
- curl from an in-cluster debug pod to the Service returns the expected HTML.

Notes and recommendations
- If you actually require pods to run only on GPU/production nodes, reintroduce the nodeSelector and label an appropriate node, e.g.:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- For clarity, consider updating the containerPort in the Deployment to 8080 and adding probes:
  - readinessProbe/livenessProbe: httpGet, port 8080, path “/”.
- If you’d like, I can update the Deployment to expose containerPort 8080 and add health probes.

Current status
- Deployment: web-app-deployment — 2/2 pods Running
- Service: web-app-service — port 80 -> targetPort 8080
- In-cluster connectivity to the Service is working; the previous “connection refused” errors should cease.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster has no node with that label. The scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
- Why connection to the Service was refused: The web-app pods listen on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged default), but the Service was targeting port 80. That mismatch caused connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-6nq5x (Running)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-d4bhl (Running)

2) Fixed Service port mismatch
- Verified the pods serve HTTP on 8080.
- Updated Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service to targetPort: 8080 (Service port remains 80).
- Result: Service now returns the NGINX welcome page. A test curl from an in-cluster pod to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 succeeds.

Verification performed
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods shows both replicas Running.
- Endpoints for web-app-service point to both pods.
- curl from an in-cluster debug pod to the Service returns the expected HTML.

Notes and recommendations
- If you actually require pods to run only on GPU/production nodes, reintroduce the nodeSelector and label an appropriate node, e.g.:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- For clarity, consider updating the containerPort in the Deployment to 8080 and adding probes:
  - readinessProbe/livenessProbe: httpGet, port 8080, path “/”.
- If you’d like, I can update the Deployment to expose containerPort 8080 and add health probes.

Current status
- Deployment: web-app-deployment — 2/2 pods Running
- Service: web-app-service — port 80 -> targetPort 8080
- In-cluster connectivity to the Service is working; the previous “connection refused” errors should cease.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster has no node with that label. The scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
- Why connection to the Service was refused: The web-app pods listen on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged default), but the Service was targeting port 80. That mismatch caused connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: 2 pods are now Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-6nq5x (Running)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-d4bhl (Running)
